summary: Defines MIB objects for managing signaling on PacketCable and IPCablecom Multimedia Terminal Adapters using SNMP. It provides a basic set of managed objects for those devices. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives cable companies a standard control panel for the little boxes that turn internet into home phone service.

questions: how to manage a cable voice adapter with snmp
what is the packetcable signaling mib
what is an mta in cable voice
what is the default ncs call agent port
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets cable operators inspect and tune call signaling on PacketCable and IPCablecom voice adapters.

tldr.problem: Cable operators run voice adapters from many vendors in many countries, and they need one standard way to manage how those devices handle call signaling.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the PKTC-IETF-SIG-MIB module, with device-wide objects (codecs, tones, ring cadences, caller ID and DSCP defaults) and a per-endpoint table of call agent and timer settings, plus compliance groups.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard MIB rooted at mib-2 169, and it was later updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 5098 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9141, so check that RFC for changes to this MIB.

sections.title: Managing Cable Voice Adapters
sections.content:
A multimedia terminal adapter (MTA) delivers broadband Internet, data and/or voice access, together with telephony service, to a customer's premises over a cable network. It sits at the customer's home and connects to the cable operator (the multiple system operator, or MSO) over a hybrid fiber coax (HFC) access network.

An MTA has one or more endpoints, for example telephone ports, which receive call signaling information to establish ring cadence and the codecs used for telephony. Telephone systems are complex and widely distributed, so management systems need to handle MTAs from several vendors and countries at once. This MIB module offers objects to manage MTA signaling in the widest possible range of markets. It is written for the Simple Network Management Protocol (RFC 3410 describes the management framework) using SMIv2.
sections.plainLanguage: People who run cable networks look after thousands of little phone boxes in homes. They need one common way to check and adjust each box, no matter who built it.

sections.title: MTAs, Endpoints and Line Packages
sections.content:
An MTA is a PacketCable- or IPCablecom-compliant device that provides telephony over a cable system. It contains an interface to endpoints, a network interface, codecs and the signaling and encapsulation functions needed for Voice-over-IP transport, call signaling and Quality of Service signaling. An Embedded MTA (E-MTA) contains a DOCSIS cable modem. A Standalone MTA (S-MTA) is separated from the cable modem by a non-DOCSIS MAC interface such as Ethernet or USB.

An endpoint is a standard telephony physical port on the MTA for attaching a telephone.

The MIB also uses two MGCP package names. The L line package is the core signaling functionality; an MTA provides all L package elements and the operator decides how they are applied. The E line package holds extensions for international requirements. Its elements are optional, vary by country and are set by operator or regulatory requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint is the socket where you plug in a phone. The L package is the basic set of phone features every box has, and the E package is extra features that depend on the country.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is named PKTC-IETF-SIG-MIB and identified as pktcIetfSigMib. It is intended to update several Signaling MIB modules from which it is partly derived: the PacketCable 1.0 and 1.5 Signaling MIB specifications, the ITU-T IPCablecom Signaling MIB requirements and the ETSI Signaling MIB. Where PacketCable and IPCablecom requirements are equivalent, the PacketCable reference is used in each object's REFERENCE clause.

It has two major parts. pktcSigMibObjects holds signaling information that controls device and endpoint configuration, and pktcSigConformance holds conformance information. Future notification objects are allowed under pktcSigNotification. Within the first part, pktcSigDevObjects covers the whole device and pktcSigEndPntConfigObjects covers each endpoint.

Endpoints are told apart through the ifTable from the IF-MIB (RFC 2863), where each ifIndex value is one endpoint. Differentiated Services Code Point values use the type from RFC 3289.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel has a section for settings that belong to the whole box and a section for settings that belong to each phone socket. Each socket is found by its number.

sections.title: Device and Endpoint Objects
sections.content:
Device-wide objects include a codec table that must list every combination of voice codecs the MTA can run at the same time, and flags saying whether the device can do echo cancellation and silence suppression. They also include the caller ID signaling protocol (FSK by default, or DTMF), user-defined ring cadences (R0 to R7, Rg and Rs), the default DSCP values for call signaling and for the media stream, a signaling capability table, tone tables and tables for pulse signals, caller ID and visual message waiting. Many of these read-write device values MUST NOT persist across MTA reboots.

A ring cadence is an octet string. After three reserved octets, each bit stands for 50 milliseconds, with 1 meaning ring tone present and 0 meaning absent. The first two reserved octets give the length in bits, from 1 to 264. The third is 0x80 for non-repeatable or 0x00 for repeatable. The MTA MUST reject sets that break these rules.

Per-endpoint settings live in pktcSigEndPntConfigTable. Each row has the call agent name and its UDP port (default 2727), many timeouts for tones and dialing, retry and timer parameters, hook flash and pulse dial timing, and status objects. A row for an endpoint means it is provisioned with voice service. The MTA updates the call agent name and port from the Notified Entity parameter of NCS messages, so changing them over SNMP is not advised during normal operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some settings are for the whole box, like which voice formats it knows. Others are for each phone socket, like how long to keep playing a busy tone. A ring pattern is stored like a row of tiny blocks, each one meaning ring or quiet for a short moment.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The conformance section defines groups of objects that an MTA must implement to claim compliance. pktcSigDeviceGroup holds the per-device objects and pktcSigEndpointGroup holds the per-endpoint objects. pktcLLinePackageGroup covers the L line package and pktcELinePackageGroup covers the E line package. pktcInternationalGroup contains optional objects designed to support operation across the widest possible range of markets.

This split lets a device in one country implement the core objects and only those international objects that its regulators or operator require.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a checklist. Every box must tick the basic items, and boxes sold in some countries also tick extra items for that country.

sections.title: Tone Table Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples of how tones are described with two tables. Each row of pktcSigDevMultiFreqToneTable describes one segment: up to four frequencies, a mode, a level in tenths of dBm, an on duration and an off duration. Each row of pktcSigDevToneTable says how many of those rows form a group and how often to repeat the group.

Example A is a call waiting tone per ITU-T E.180, built from a 400 Hz tone modulated by 16 Hz plus short 400 Hz bursts, assigned to userDefined1(18). It uses five multi-frequency rows grouped by one tone row that plays only once. Example B is a congestion tone that repeats two segments up to 5000 times or until the T0 timeout, whichever is shorter. Example C is a call waiting tone made of two groups: the first plays once, and the second repeats.
sections.plainLanguage: A beep pattern is described as a list of steps like 'play this note for half a second, then stay quiet for a while'. Another small list says how many steps go together and whether to loop them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and allowing SET operations without protection can harm network operation. Specific cases are called out. If the DSCP objects (pktcSigDefCallSigDscp and pktcSigDefMediaStreamDscp) are set maliciously, unmarked or wrongly marked traffic may enter the provider network and customers may get unauthorized service levels. If the ring cadence, caller ID protocol and pulse signal objects are altered, devices may behave wrongly or fail to get telephony service. If the call agent name or UDP port is changed, the MTA cannot reach its call agent and telephony is disrupted.

Some readable objects are also sensitive. pktcSigEndPntStatusCallIpAddress is called the most sensitive, pktcSigEndPntStatusError can help impersonators, and pktcSigDevCodecMax can help plan denial-of-service attacks.

Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 lack adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and leaves it to operators to grant access only to legitimate principals.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could change the settings, phones might stop ringing or stop connecting. So only trusted people should be allowed in, and the messages should be locked up with SNMPv3.
